title: Optimize distance calculations:  consider replacing sf::st_distance
description:
Hi there!

Just a short note on the distance calculations. From my experience, it's one of the major bottlenecks in the package. For example, I can't even apply the `spatialsample` package for my datasets with 40k points in it.

https://github.com/tidymodels/spatialsample/blob/ded16914d80c5bb118d8a61ffd93e07be5aad93e/R/buffer.R#L27

What if we replace `sf::st_distance` with a slightly more robust function? For example, [there is some evidence](https://kadyb.github.io/geotips/html/01_distance_between_points.html) that `Rfast::Dist` works two to three times faster than `sf::st_distance()`. Perhaps it would be worth adding one more package to the dependency list in the name of a speed boost?

Unfortunately, both algorithms seem to have O(n²) time complexity, which is not good, and `Rfast` is not a silver bullet. Additionally, in the case of longlat coordinates, `sf::st_distance()` may still be preferable as it computes Great Circle distance.

I can prepare a PR if you like the approach.

See below some benchmarking

``` r
library(sf)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.12.1, GDAL 3.8.4, PROJ 9.3.1; sf_use_s2() is TRUE
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(Rfast))
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(bench)

# Function to create points
create_points <- function(n) {
  bbox <- sf::st_bbox(c(
    xmin = 1400000, xmax = 2100000,
    ymin = 5400000, ymax = 6200000
  ))
  bbox <- sf::st_as_sfc(bbox)
  sf::st_crs(bbox) <- 2193
  sf::st_sample(bbox, n)
}

# Run benchmarks for different n
ns <- seq(1000, 10000, by = 1000)
results <- list()

for (n in ns) {
  set.seed(n)
  pts <- create_points(n)

  bm <- bench::mark(
    sf = sf::st_distance(pts, which = "Euclidean"),
    Rfast = pts |>
      sf::st_coordinates() |>
      Rfast::Dist(method = "euclidean"),
    time_unit = "ms",
    iterations = 5,
    check = FALSE
  )

  # Add n to the results
  bm$n <- n
  results[[as.character(n)]] <- bm
}

# Combine and prepare results
benchmark_df <- do.call(rbind, results)

# Reshape for faceted plotting
plot_df <-
  benchmark_df |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    n,
    method = as.character(expression),
    time = as.numeric(median),
    mem_alloc = as.numeric(mem_alloc)
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(time, mem_alloc),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric = factor(metric,
      levels = c("time", "mem_alloc"),
      labels = c("Time (milliseconds)", "Memory (bytes)")
    )
  )


# Plot the results
plot_df |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = n, y = value, color = method)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = ns) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 5),
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y", nrow = 2) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "sf vs Rfast Distance Calculations",
    y = "",
    x = "Number of Points",
    color = "Method"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")
  )
#> `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'

title: “All models failed” with spatial_block_cv() + tune_grid() — “arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1” error
description:
### Brief description of the problem

I am experiencing an error when using **spatial_block_cv()** from **{spatialsample}** together with **{tidymodels}**' tune_grid() to perform spatial cross-validation on my dataset. The same dataset and modeling approach works fine with a standard `vfold_cv()`, but fails in all folds with an error message:

Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE): arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1 Error in estimate_tune_results(): ! All models failed. Run show_notes(.Last.tune.result) for more information.


I have verified the following:

1. **No empty folds**: I checked `analysis()` and `assessment()` sets in each fold; they all have >0 rows and include both classes (0 and 1).  
2. **No recipe issues**: I removed all recipe steps (including `step_corr()` and `step_zv()`), or even removed the recipe entirely, and the error persists.  
3. **Simple model**: I tested a non-tunable `rand_forest` model with `fit_resamples()` (i.e., no hyperparameter grid) and still see the same failure.  
4. **vfold_cv()** works: If I switch from `spatial_block_cv()` to `vfold_cv()`, the model + data run successfully through `tune_grid()` or `fit_resamples()` with no errors.  
5. **Indices look correct**: The number of rows in `analysis()` and `assessment()` is consistent across folds, each includes humedal == 0 and humedal == 1, so no single-class or 0-row subsets.  
6. **Tried reducing folds / radius**: For instance, `v=3` or `radius=50` instead of `v=5` and `radius=100`. The same error arises.  
7. **Tried removing geometry**: I used a typical approach of reassigning splits with `make_splits()` to remove geometry from each fold’s analysis/assessment sets, and forced `class(...) <- class(folds_spatial)`. The error persists.  

### Repro steps and partial code

Below is a simplified version of my workflow:

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(spatialsample)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

# Example: I have ~827 data points (presence/absence)
# plus 4 raster-based predictors: ndvi, mndwi, pendiente, ti
# My dataset is an sf object with geometry.

# 1) I create folds:
set.seed(1996)
folds_spatial <- spatial_block_cv(
  data   = my_data_sf,   # ~827 points
  v      = 5,
  radius = 100
)

# 2) Drop geometry in each split:
my_data_nogeo <- st_drop_geometry(my_data_sf)

folds_spatial_nogeo <- folds_spatial %>%
  mutate(
    splits = map(splits, function(s) {
      i_ana <- s$in_id
      i_ass <- s$out_id
      
      rsample::make_splits(
        x    = list(analysis = i_ana, assessment = i_ass),
        data = my_data_nogeo,
        class= "spatial_block_split"
      )
    })
  )
# Restore class
class(folds_spatial_nogeo) <- class(folds_spatial)

# 3) Model specification
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("ranger", probability = TRUE)

my_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(rf_spec)
  # (Sometimes I add a recipe, or none.)

set.seed(1996)
res <- fit_resamples(
  my_wf,
  resamples = folds_spatial_nogeo
)
# -> Fails with:
# Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE) : arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1
# All models failed.
```

I also tried tune_grid() with a small grid of mtry and min_n and got the same result (All models failed).

Observations / Diagnostics
- If I switch to vfold_cv(my_data_nogeo, v=5, strata=humedal), everything works.
- The dataset is not huge, but I do have enough rows in each fold (I double-checked with a for loop printing nrow(analysis(...)), nrow(assessment(...)) and the distribution of humedal).
- Reducing to v=2 or v=3, or changing radius from 100 to 50, did not help.
- Removing any recipe steps or hyperparameter tuning also did not help.

title: `spatial_clustering_cv` retains geometry in folds causing `fit_resamples` to fail
description:
## The problem

When using `spatial_clustering_cv` to create spatial resamples, the geometry column is retained within the folds. This causes `fit_resamples` to fail with an error indicating that not all columns of y are known outcome types. It's unclear whether `spatial_clustering_cv` should drop the spatial information in the folds or if `fit_resamples` should exclude the geometry information. There might be something I'm missing.

## Reproducible example

``` r
# Load package

title: Is spatialsample ready for v1.0.0?
description:
I think spatialsample is ready for version 1.0.0. We're building on top of rsample >= 1.0.0, which has had a pretty stable interface for multiple years, and I'd be surprised myself if much of the interface or the returned objects changed in the future.

The main reasons spatialsample _wouldn't_ be 1.0.0 ready that I can think of would be:

+ Stratification isn't supported, and isn't currently on the short-term roadmap (but might be in the future). This might cause a big change to the package.
+ `spatial_nndm_cv()` is still somewhat experimental and might change in the future, as the team that introduced NNDM is talking about proposing a V-fold variant.

Still, I think we're in a place where the next release could be a 1.0.0 release. I'm opening this issue to see what others think!

title: With `prediction_sites` as a single polygon, `spatial_nndm_cv()` produces a LOOCV
description:
## The problem

Related to #145 
I think there's a bug when passing a polygon as `prediction_sites` to `spatial_nndm_cv`. When I use a single single sfc_POLYGON, the assessment folds do not have any buffer around them -- the CV just becomes a LOOCV. When I pass a sfc_POINT object sampled from the same sfc_POLYGON, the NNDM has folds as expected. 

Wrapping the sfc_POLYGON in a call to `st_sample` is of course a very easy workaround, but the documentation clearly states the desired behavior for a single polygon. 

Having looked quickly at the source code, it seems to me that `sample_points` is not being carried forward as the `prediction_sites` (unless it lacks a CRS). https://github.com/tidymodels/spatialsample/blob/9877514c909ed063d34e64a11365b400b218b394/R/spatial_nndm_cv.R#L131

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(sf)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.12.1, GDAL 3.8.4, PROJ 9.3.1; sf_use_s2() is TRUE
library(spatialsample)
data(ames, package = "modeldata")

ames_sf <- st_as_sf(ames, coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)

# Passing prediction_sites as single sfc_POLYGON
ch <- st_concave_hull(st_union(ames_sf), ratio = 0.4, allow_holes = TRUE)
str(ch)
#> sfc_POLYGON of length 1; first list element: List of 2
#>  $ : num [1:72, 1:2] -93.7 -93.7 -93.7 -93.7 -93.7 ...
#>  $ : num [1:6, 1:2] -93.6 -93.6 -93.6 -93.6 -93.6 ...
#>  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:3] "XY" "POLYGON" "sfg"

set.seed(123)
nndm <- spatial_nndm_cv(ames_sf[1:100, ], ch) 
print(nndm, n=2)
#> # A tibble: 100 × 2
#>   splits         id     
#>   <list>         <chr>  
#> 1 <split [99/1]> Fold001
#> 2 <split [99/1]> Fold002
#> # ℹ 98 more rows
foldN <- nndm |> 
  rsample::tidy() |> 
  dplyr::count(Resample) |> 
  dplyr::pull(n)
all(foldN == 100)
#> [1] TRUE
autoplot(get_rsplit(nndm, 1))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/wdyQON7.png)<!-- -->

``` r

# Passing prediction_sites as sfc_POINT
set.seed(123)
chpts <- st_sample(ch, size = 1000)
str(chpts)
#> sfc_POINT of length 1000; first list element:  'XY' num [1:2] -93.7 42

set.seed(123)
nndm2 <- spatial_nndm_cv(ames_sf[1:100, ], chpts) 
print(nndm2, n=2)
#> # A tibble: 100 × 2
#>   splits         id     
#>   <list>         <chr>  
#> 1 <split [50/1]> Fold001
#> 2 <split [50/1]> Fold002
#> # ℹ 98 more rows
autoplot(get_rsplit(nndm2, 1))
```

title: If `prediction_sites` are a single polygon, `spatial_nndm_cv()` should sample within that polygon, not within the bounding box
description:
## Feature

If you have a prediction area that's not very square, it would make sense that you'd want your sample "prediction sites" (used for estimating autocorrelation functions) to be within your actual prediction area, not its (much larger) bounding box. Right now, for any non-point prediction sites, we sample within the bounding box:

https://github.com/tidymodels/spatialsample/blob/4bf6dffcf116e39dac4aa644ba1b55a9c580df77/R/spatial_nndm_cv.R#L114-L126

But if `prediction_sites` is of length 1 and a polygon, I think it would be nicer to sample within _that_ polygon, rather than the bounding box of the polygon.

(The workaround, for anyone seeing this before it's closed, is to sample within your polygon yourself and pass those points to `prediction_sites` instead)

description:
## Feature

It would be nice if spatialsample re-exported functions like get_rsplit(), and possibly analysis() and assessment(), so that spatialsample could be used on its own without also needing to load rsample (either via library() or `::`). 

If those functions were re-exported, it might also be useful to re-export a handful of other one-off utilities. I'm thinking rsample::reshuffle_rset() and _maybe_ rsample::reverse_splits(), though I don't entirely remember the original use-case for that function.

title: Test reshuffle_rsplits on spatialsample objects (once released)
Parallelize buffering via `furrr`
description:
## Feature

Buffering takes a _while_. For making one rset, it's not that bad, but when making multiple (particularly with many rsplits) it becomes a huge timesink. The process is almost entirely CPU limited.

That said, we apply buffering to each rsplit completely independently (buffers in one resample are irrelevant to the next). I think one way to dramatically speed up this process would be to change this line from `purrr` to `furrr`, enabling users to parallelize buffering via `future`:
https://github.com/tidymodels/spatialsample/blob/02a654adcecbb6e05bcbf532692350fba4e842cc/R/buffer.R#L47

The downside is that if this is inside of _other_ parallel workflows (for instance, inside a targets script that's already using `future`) it could wind up causing problems. 

What do others think?

title: There should be a standard way to set `v` to `max_v`
description:
## Feature

spatialsample uses a different check_v than rsample, because it's often the case that setting v to max_v makes statistical sense (in situations like leave-one-block-out CV, leave-one-location-out CV, and so on). However, it can be difficult to know in advance what `v` _should_ be for these circumstances, for instance to know how many blocks will contain data in the process of running spatial_block_cv. Right now, my general approach is to set `v = Inf`, which works with a warning:

``` r
library(spatialsample)

spatial_block_cv(boston_canopy, v = Inf)
#> Warning in spatial_block_cv(boston_canopy, v = Inf): Fewer than Inf blocks available for sampling
#> ℹ Setting `v` to 61
#> #  61-fold spatial block cross-validation 
#> # A tibble: 61 × 2
#>    splits           id    
#>    <list>           <chr> 
#>  1 <split [665/17]> Fold01
#>  2 <split [679/3]>  Fold02
#>  3 <split [666/16]> Fold03
#>  4 <split [665/17]> Fold04
#>  5 <split [674/8]>  Fold05
#>  6 <split [671/11]> Fold06
#>  7 <split [676/6]>  Fold07
#>  8 <split [679/3]>  Fold08
#>  9 <split [665/17]> Fold09
#> 10 <split [671/11]> Fold10
#> # … with 51 more rows
```

<sup>Created on 2022-06-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

I think this makes good, intuitive sense, and gives the expected result: we're setting `v` higher than the maximum acceptable number of folds and getting `max_v` instead, and by setting `v` to infinity we can be sure it's higher than that maximum. I think we shouldn't warn when `is.infinite(v)` and document this as the supported way to perform leave-one-something-out CV.

An alternative would be to use `NULL` for this special case, which [is how rsample does it in group vfold](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/reference/group_vfold_cv.html) and might be a more normal "special case" value than Inf, which I bet a good chunk of users are barely aware of in the first place. Right now this errors:

``` r
library(spatialsample)

spatial_block_cv(boston_canopy, v = NULL)
#> Error in `spatial_block_cv()`:
#> ! `v` must be a single positive integer.
```

<sup>Created on 2022-06-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

`NULL` feels less graceful to me for this purpose than `Inf`, but might be more idiomatic.

Is this enough of a problem that we should save `boston_canopy` as a data.frame, rather than a tibble?

title: We could signal silly grids better
description:
## The problem

It's a little too easy right now to create silly grids. For instance, using our Boston data set:

``` r
library(spatialsample)
x <- spatial_block_cv(boston_canopy, n = c(200, 200), v = Inf)
#> Warning in spatial_block_cv(boston_canopy, n = c(200, 200), v = Inf): Fewer than Inf blocks available for sampling
#> ℹ Setting `v` to 682
autoplot(x) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")
#> Coordinate system already present. Adding new coordinate system, which will replace the existing one.
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/zi8LcOb.png)

This grid is obviously mis-matched to the data, since 98% of blocks are getting thrown out. However, it's not wild to think that sometimes you _expect_ the majority of blocks to get thrown away; for instance when blocking with island data:

``` r
boston_canopy[grep("^(A-|B|C|D|E|F|G|AQ|AP|AO|AN|AN|AL)", boston_canopy$grid_id), ] |> 
  spatial_block_cv() |> 
  autoplot()
#> Coordinate system already present. Adding new coordinate system, which will replace the existing one.
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/0MJTRpT.png)

<sup>Created on 2022-06-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

It'd be nice to have some messaging around this situation. Two possibilities:

* Have an `rlang::inform()` call send a message whenever more than a certain threshold of blocks are thrown away

title: buffer_indices doesn't work with units objects
description:
## The problem

So I missed this in the course of review on #39, but part of the reason I checked for `radius` via `if (radius)` (and buffer via `if (dist)`) was because it let us pass `units` objects to control scales. This doesn't work anymore now that we test for `> 0`

``` r
x <- 1
if (x) TRUE
#> [1] TRUE
if (x > 0)
x <- units::as_units(x, "m")
if (x) TRUE
#> [1] TRUE
if (x > 0) TRUE
#> Error in Ops.units(x, 0): both operands of the expression should be "units" objects
```
The simple fix is to strip the units when comparing against 0. We should also test to make sure adding units works for both `radius` and `buffer` so this can't get broken accidentally again.

title: Autoplot for `spatial_block_cv()` with geographic data draws the wrong grid
description:
## The problem

The autoplot method for `spatial_block_cv()` draws a grid which is completely mis-aligned with the actual splits produced:

`set.seed(123); spatial_block_cv(ames_sf, v = 2, method = "continuous") |> autoplot()`

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/38229299/172739980-35c63a5a-8318-4dde-9a86-4e791449ba5a.png)

With `method = continuous`, these blocks should be alternating colors; they clearly are not.

However, under the hood it _appears_ that folds are being created as expected. For instance, dropping into a `debug()` session here:
https://github.com/tidymodels/spatialsample/blob/d271211c0ca7de268f42b1715e1a9eb09a2edd37/R/spatial_block_cv.R#L107

And running `plot(sf::st_geometry(data)); plot(grid_blocks, add = TRUE)` produces:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/38229299/172740434-f9fa3814-19d5-4d81-93fe-8883a0b909ee.png)

The grid lines align with the folds, which are assigned from left to right correctly. Based on _this_ grid, the folds are correct.

This means that somewhere in `autoplot()` the new grid is being drawn incorrectly, and should be updated. 

It's worth flagging that this means the default grid being used is very different based on if the data is geographic or projected. For instance, with `ames` in a projected CRS, we get:

`set.seed(123); spatial_block_cv(sf::st_transform(ames_sf, 5070), v = 2, method = "continuous") |> autoplot()`

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/38229299/172740868-2950efdc-d914-4595-a71e-07e6d69dafdb.png)

This has the behavior I expect from not passing arguments to `make_grid`: 10 cells in each direction. 

This might come down to trying to ensure points are "within" the straight lines of their bounding box while on a spherical surface:
https://github.com/tidymodels/spatialsample/blob/d271211c0ca7de268f42b1715e1a9eb09a2edd37/R/spatial_block_cv.R#L94

title: Disc-based CV
description:
The next method in line is disc-based partitioning, as implemented in `sperrorest`:
https://giscience-fsu.github.io/sperrorest/reference/partition_disc.html

The way that `sperrorest` works is:

+ You set a number of "discs" to create. There is one disc per test set. 
+ For each "disc", a random data point is selected
+ All data within a set radius of that point is in `test`
+ All data within a set buffer radius around the test set is excluded entirely
+ All other data is in `train`

With radius set to 0 and `nrow(data)` "discs", this is equivalent to LOOCV with a buffer around the test point. If you increase the radius, more points will be in `test`, but there's only ever one disc per test set.

I think it might be useful to change that slightly. I'm basically thinking of having a function along the lines of:

`spatial_disc_cv(data, v, radius, buffer, max_discs)`

Where `v` controls the number of folds, and `max_discs` the number of discs per fold. If you set `max_discs` to 1, then you get one disc per fold, just like in `sperrorest`. If you leave it as `NULL` then you instead get `nrow(data) / v` discs per fold. For `radius = 0` this is equivalent to a v-fold CV with buffering around the test set.

For small `v` with large radii/buffers this might result in too much data in `test` and not enough in `train`, and we might need heuristics to warn in those situations. 

To be clear, I haven't seen my proposed change anywhere in the literature (though I haven't looked _that_ intensely). It just feels like a natural extension to better match the rest of our resampling functions, which typically leave multiple locations out at a time. What do people think?

title: Functions have different argument names representing the same concept
description:
I want to flag this now while it's still changeable (neither of these have hit CRAN yet): the argument controlling how clusters are made is named `cluster_function`, while the argument controlling how blocks are made is named `method`:

https://github.com/tidymodels/spatialsample/blob/710737a32b1a0dc0d06f9ac2c94a2eee8970867e/R/spatial_clustering_cv.R#L24

https://github.com/tidymodels/spatialsample/blob/710737a32b1a0dc0d06f9ac2c94a2eee8970867e/R/spatial_block_cv.R#L27

This feels a little uneven, because different functions in the package don't have the same general names for doing the same general things. 

Now, `spatial_clustering_cv` can't use `method`, because we want to pass that to either `kmeans` or `hclust` via `...`. And I don't think changing `method` to `blocking_function` or similar makes sense, because it's not _actually_ a function in the same sense. But I wanted to flag this to see if others think it's an issue, and if they can think of a better argument name that we can use for this role across the package.

title: Nearest neighbor distance matching LOOCV
description:
## Feature

This is a relatively novel approach for spatial CV, introduced by Edzer Pebesma and Hanna Meyer alongside Jorge Mateu and Carles Milà. The approach is pretty simple -- calculate the nearest neighbor G, set up for LOOCV, and remove points from each test fold until the G for the test data to the training data approximates that for the entire data set. (I might be mis-stating that).

Might be worth including! I think we're agreed that determining autocorrelation distance is out of scope, but calculating nearest neighbor distance internally for this function is somewhat trivial.

https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13851

title: Add buffer arguments to spatial CV functions
description:
## Feature

Often, spatial CV in the literature will exclude points within a "buffer" radius around points assigned to the test fold, so as to further reduce spatial autocorrelation between the training and testing data. For instance, from MuseoToolbox:

![Image showing a spatial exclusion buffer around the included points](https://museotoolbox.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_images/sphx_glr_SpatialLeaveOneSubGroupOut_001.png)

Because this functionality is somewhat generic across methods, it would make sense for us to implement buffers similarly to how `rsample` implements strata, as a lower-level function that has standard behavior throughout the package.

title: spatial_block_cv assigns polygons to every block they touch, not just the one their centroid falls in
description:
## The problem

`spatial_block_cv` assigns polygons to every block they touch, meaning that a single polygon will often be used in multiple test sets. I don't know if this is _undesirable_ behavior, but it was _surprising_, and I think it'd make sense to talk about what people would expect to happen in this situation.

If we want to not duplicate polygons across folds, then the simple fix is to assign based on centroid position (via `sf::st_centroid`) which should automatically fix this. Running `st_centroid` on a point geometry returns the same point, so we could apply that without needing to check geometry type. 

I bet this also happens with other geometry types (lines, etc) but I'm not sure when people are fitting models to those.

## Reproducible example

This data set has 682 rows, but note how many more test observations there are than that. You can see the effect in the autoplot plot, based on how many hexagons appear to be in the last few folds (because only the "top" fold is displayed):

``` r
library(spatialsample)

set.seed(123)
blocked <- spatial_block_cv(boston_canopy, n = c(20, 20))

My background is geology and hydrogeology where we often have categorical predictors such as geological unit, land use class, soil type etc. The spatial sizes and distributions of classes can be highly imbalanced. For this reason it is often not possible to use spatial resampling without stratification because there is always the danger, that samples from smaller or more rare classes end up in only one of the splits.
Maybe this could be implemented at some point in the future. I would really appreciate it.
Anyways, I really like the work you are doing and looking forward to what will come.

That will be preceded by a release of the [usethis package](https://usethis.r-lib.org), which will gain some functionality around detecting and adapting to a renamed default branch. There will also be a blog post at the time of this `master` --> `main` change.

The purpose of this issue is to:

* Help us firm up the list of targetted repositories
* Make sure all maintainers are aware of what's coming
* Give us an issue to close when the job is done
* Give us a place to put advice for collaborators re: how to adapt

title: Consider reversing `coords` and `v` in signature
description:
Rather than 

```r
spatial_clustering_cv(data, v = 10, coords, ...)
```

consider

```r
spatial_clustering_cv(data, coords, v = 10, ...)
```

Since `coords` have to be specified, the first approach forces you to specify `v` even though it is an optional argument.

The second approach lets you do `spatial_clustering_cv(data, c(Lat, Long))` without specifying `v`, which I think is kind of nice.

In general, I always put required args up front, then optional ones, possibly separating the two groups of args with `...` if they aren't being used to force the user to specify optional ones by name. This is a little like the "data, dots, details" design principle, but obviously the dots here are used to pass on to `kmeans()`, and they should stay at the back. https://design.tidyverse.org/dots-position.html
